title: A distribution over functions, updating
sub: GP regression with an RBF kernel on noisy samples of a wiggly function.

frames.caption: Before any data: the prior, a GP with an RBF kernel (ℓ = 1). The shaded band is ±2 standard deviations; the thin aqua lines are three functions drawn from the prior. The dashed line is the true function, which the GP never sees.

One noisy observation at x = 2. The posterior must pass near it, so the band pinches there. Further than a couple of length scales away, nothing has changed: the kernel says distant points are nearly unrelated.
A second point at x = 7.5. The mean (blue) is a kernel-weighted combination of the observations; between the two points it relaxes back towards the prior mean of 0.
Four points. Every sampled function now has to thread through all of them, and they agree wherever data is dense.

Eight points: the posterior mean tracks the true function closely, and the band is narrow near data and widens only in the gaps and at the edges. That uncertainty map is what Bayesian optimization uses to decide where to look next.

Same eight points, length scale ℓ = 0.25: the GP assumes the function can change a lot over a short distance, so it fits each point but snaps back to 0 between them. The marginal likelihood is a little lower: the fit is fine, but the extra flexibility is penalized.
ℓ = 1: smooth enough to bridge the gaps, flexible enough to follow the bumps. This has the highest marginal likelihood of the three, though only slightly ahead of ℓ = 0.25.

ℓ = 4: the GP insists the function varies slowly, so it cannot follow the fast wiggle and treats it as noise. The marginal likelihood drops again: too rigid. Maximizing it over ℓ is how GP hyperparameters are usually learned.
